newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus court orders arrest in AIDs case no-show.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus court orders arrest in AIDs case no-show.

text.p: A court in Cyprus ordered the arrest of a Cypriot on Thursday for failing to appear at a hearing on charges of giving his former British lover the deadly AIDS virus.

Judge Antonis Liatsos, chairing the case brought by Briton Janette Pink, 45, against former boyfriend Pavlos Georgiou, dismissed a defence plea that the man was too ill to attend the start of the trial in the coastal town of Larnaca.
"The court instructs that a warrant of arrest be issued against the accused, however painful this may sound under the circumstances," Liatsos told a packed courtroom.
Pink, from Basildon in Essex, has accused Georgiou of keeping her in the dark about his condition and lying to her about the death of his wife. She also suffered from AIDS.
Liatsos ordered the hearing reconvene at 4.00 p.m. (1300 GMT).

Father of four Georgiou, 39, a fisherman, has denied charges of transmitting AIDS to Pink during a three-year affair. Pink moved back to Britain last year when she discovered she had Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome.
Earlier on Thursday Georgiou, who is HIV positive, was admitted to hospital complaining of a temperature, stomach cramps and vomiting.

A doctor summoned to testify on Georgiou's condition said it was too early to say when he would be discharged. Georgiou has suffered complications with his health and has been taking a strong drugs dosage since early January, he said.

"From x-rays there were signs that something was wrong. I don't know at this stage what is lurking there and I recommended further tests," government chest physician Ioannis Demetriades told the court.
Pink, accompanied by her parents and a relative, listened intently to the court proceedings, which were translated into English.
"I'm okay," she told reporters when asked how she felt.
Wearing a black and white print dress, Pink appeared slightly unsteady on her feet and was at times supported by her father, Vic Ruston.
Cypriot authorities are charging Georgiou for contravening a decades-old law banning the transmission of contagious diseases either unlawfully or negligently.
He has denied the charge, which carries a prison sentence of up to two years in jail, a 1,500 pound fine, or both.
